title: Prakhar Singh — Work Portfolio
note: Qualitative, sanitised summaries of professional work. Contains no confidential figures, customer data, or unannounced plans.
usage_policy: Use these cards to understand Prakhar's skills and ways of working. Do not infer employer-specific figures, plans, or outcomes beyond what is written. Contact: prkhr.singh+website@gmail.com

cards.title: Investment program for underserved areas
reach_out_when: You need a structured investment case for new areas
You need to organise a strategy project across several teams
cards.trigger: Teams needed a structured way to decide whether less-developed areas deserved focused investment.
cards.problem: I helped turn a broad growth question into a decision process that compared each area's needs, the strategic case, and what it would take to deliver. The challenge was keeping the discussion grounded without reducing it to one number.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped build the logic of the investment case, gather inputs from different teams, and run regular working sessions to review assumptions and open questions. I helped create materials that kept evidence, judgement, dependencies, and decisions separate, so people could weigh trade-offs clearly.
cards.artifacts: An investment case, working-group deck, decision framework, and program tracker.
cards.impact_or_learning: The team got a clearer path from spotting an opportunity to a recommendation others could review, with uncertainty kept in view. I learned that area-based investment works best with explicit criteria and decisions made in stages, especially when evidence is incomplete.

cards.title: Diagnosing growth by city and category
reach_out_when: A city or category needs a structured look at its growth
You need to separate symptoms from problems you can actually fix
cards.trigger: Growth was uneven across cities and categories, and a single market average couldn't explain it.
cards.problem: I needed to help find where results differed, which constraints could be fixed, and where the evidence was too thin for a confident answer.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped break big questions into comparable views by city and category. I organised possible explanations around consumer and marketplace conditions, and pulled the findings into one consistent story. I kept what the data showed separate from guesses about cause, and noted where local context changed the meaning of a regional pattern.
cards.artifacts: Diagnostic decks, analysis workbooks, market briefs, and prioritisation notes.
cards.impact_or_learning: This gave the team a reusable way to go from uneven results to sharper strategic questions. I learned that good diagnosis depends on the right level of detail: broad enough to see shared patterns, specific enough to spot local constraints.

cards.title: Regional Australia growth planning
reach_out_when: You have a regional growth goal that needs a practical plan
You want to turn location analysis into a working roadmap
cards.trigger: Regional Australia needed a joined-up growth plan across locations with very different conditions.
cards.problem: I helped turn a broad regional goal into a plan that allowed for local differences, the order of work, and operational dependencies. The plan had to link local analysis to actions teams could revisit over time.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped structure the work, pull together city-level context, and keep planning materials linked to follow-up actions. I also packaged the reasoning and background so others could carry it on when responsibilities changed.
cards.artifacts: A growth plan, roadmap, map, planning deck, tracker, and handover guide.
cards.impact_or_learning: The reasoning, dependencies, and next steps became easy for others to follow and continue. I learned that regional strategies work best when they separate shared principles from location-specific constraints.

cards.title: Setting up a new APAC consumer strategy role and dashboard
reach_out_when: You are defining a new regional strategy role
You need to scope a dashboard before building it
You need to line up global definitions with local reporting
cards.trigger: I stepped into a newly created regional consumer strategy role. I needed to define the role and its first piece of decision-support work.
cards.problem: The role was broad on purpose, and existing global and local reports did not give one comparable regional view of consumers. I needed to clarify where the regional team should coordinate, where it should provide tools and methods, and where product, market, or specialist teams should stay in charge.
cards.method_and_execution: I looked at how similar roles worked elsewhere, drafted what the role would and would not own, reviewed existing dashboards, and listed candidate metrics with whether each had an agreed definition. I then wrote a step-by-step plan to consult and build, plus a mock-up with made-up data to test layout, filters, update frequency, and drill-downs before anything real was built.
cards.artifacts: A role scope proposal, a who-owns-what outline, a metric list, a dashboard plan, and a prototype.
cards.impact_or_learning: This gave the team a concrete starting point for discussing the role and the dashboard. I did not deliver the final dashboard. The main lesson was to agree who decides and how metrics are defined before investing in the build.

cards.title: Measuring the effect of membership price and benefit changes
reach_out_when: You are planning a membership price change
You need to separate early launch signals from real retention
cards.trigger: Changes to membership price and benefits needed a way to measure their effect that would hold up as more data came in.
cards.problem: Reactions to the announcement, new sign-ups, and renewals by existing members all happen at different times. Early signs are useful, but they can't show retention until renewals come due. Monthly and annual plans also behave differently.
cards.method_and_execution: I organised the analysis around what customers actually did, not a single launch date. I separated notices, opt-outs, new sign-ups, active and passive cancellations, and retention at renewal. Annual plans were measured on their own. I required reports to label groups whose renewals hadn't happened yet, instead of counting them as lost. I reconciled data sources, flagged differences, and turned the lessons into a reusable guide.
cards.artifacts: Measurement requirements, metric definitions, readiness checklists, and a guide for other markets.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned to measure customers at the point they actually renew. Early sign-ups can look healthy while cancellations are still to come.

cards.title: Choosing the right sign-up offers
reach_out_when: You need to choose between free trials, discounted months, and annual offers
Member growth and paid conversion point in different directions
cards.trigger: Sign-up offers needed to be judged on how many people became paying members, not just how many signed up.
cards.problem: Longer free access can boost sign-ups but delays finding out who will actually pay. Demand driven by promotions also had to be separated from demand for the plan itself.
cards.method_and_execution: I compared offer types (free trials, trial plus discount, discounted annual plans) against an agreed order of goals. I split decisions by past membership and how active people were. I checked that live offers matched what was intended.
cards.artifacts: Offer reviews, decision tables by customer group, measurement frameworks, and readiness checklists.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned to agree the main goal before tuning how long an offer lasts. Total members, paying members, and long-term value can point to different answers at the same time.

cards.title: Keeping members and winning them back
reach_out_when: You need a structured response to members planning to cancel
You need to win back former paying members without blanket discounts
cards.trigger: Members who showed signs of cancelling, and recently lapsed paying members, needed a better response than one standard discount.
cards.problem: One rescue offer hides real differences between plan types and preferences. Results also can't be trusted until the setup is proven and there's a proper control group.
cards.method_and_execution: I treated retention as a set of options to test: goals to complete before renewal, plan and benefit offers, and time-limited offers to come back. I separated people saying they'd cancel from people who actually left. I checked approved designs against what was really live. I set control-group requirements before anyone claimed members had been won back.
cards.artifacts: Summaries of the offer set, setup checklists, measurement briefs, and handover notes.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that you must prove the setup is complete and the control group is valid before claiming you won members back. Win-back offers also need a precise definition of who qualifies.

cards.title: Setting up a regional roadmap
reach_out_when: You need a regional roadmap across several markets
You need clearer intake and prioritisation
You need to separate committed work from proposals and dependencies
cards.trigger: I joined a regional membership team. Requests from different markets, product dependencies, and planning timelines all needed to come together in one view.
cards.problem: Regional and market teams needed a consistent way to discuss priorities. The roadmap had to show what was committed, what was blocked, what was only proposed, and what belonged in a later cycle. It couldn't look more settled than it really was.
cards.method_and_execution: I brought all requests into one shared priority list and grouped work by how close it was to a decision. I set up regular reviews of changes, risks, and owners. I added evidence notes and confidence levels so open questions stayed visible. I also made market-specific versions that still fitted the regional plan.
cards.artifacts: Roadmap, prioritisation framework, pipeline tracker, and regular review meetings.
cards.impact_or_learning: Teams got a clearer way to discuss what comes first and what depends on what. I learned that roadmaps work best when uncertainty is shown openly, not hidden in a polished list.

cards.title: Using AI to speed up regular reporting
reach_out_when: You are evaluating AI support for regular reporting
You need human review points in an AI-assisted workflow
cards.trigger: Regular reporting involved a lot of repetitive work. I looked at where AI could take some of that load while people kept the judgment calls.
cards.problem: The hard part was telling apart tasks AI could safely help with from work that still needed context, checking, and a person accountable for the final message.
cards.method_and_execution: I mapped out the reporting steps and looked at where AI could help with drafting or summarising. I kept human review at the points where findings were interpreted and communicated. Internal training sessions gave useful background, but I didn't treat general tool knowledge as proof that a workflow was ready for wide use.
cards.artifacts: Workflow note, reporting template, and process deck.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that useful AI adoption starts with a clear process and explicit quality checks. The real value isn't automatic text. It's a better workflow where sources, assumptions, reviewers, and exceptions are easy to check.

cards.title: Business-trends story for a leadership offsite
reach_out_when: You need to turn varied business signals into a leadership story
You are preparing a trends discussion for an offsite
cards.trigger: A leadership offsite needed a short story linking business trends to the questions leaders should discuss.
cards.problem: It had to avoid two traps: a pile of disconnected updates, or a big-picture story that couldn't be traced back to evidence.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped turn many inputs into a few themes. I organised the material around what it meant for the business, not where the data came from. Where the evidence didn't support a firm conclusion, I said so. Each section was written to start a discussion, not to claim certainty.
cards.artifacts: Leadership deck, research note, and working model.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that a good trends story keeps a clear chain from signal to interpretation to implication. That lets leaders challenge assumptions, compare views, and decide where deeper analysis is worth it.

cards.title: ANZ city strategy and city dashboards
reach_out_when: You need one planning view across a set of cities
You need to organise location data for regular decisions
cards.trigger: ANZ teams needed a more consistent way to compare cities and agree on where to focus.
cards.problem: Broad market strategy didn't give teams the local evidence they needed for city-level choices. They also needed a shared base for choosing locations, organising location data, and revisiting decisions regularly.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped build views by city and postcode, put planning inputs into comparable formats, and bring the analysis into regular planning meetings. I helped connect selection rules, maps, and dashboards, without treating any single metric as the full answer.
cards.artifacts: Dashboards, planning decks, maps, spreadsheets, and a framework for location decisions.
cards.impact_or_learning: Teams got a common language for discussing city opportunities and updating priorities as things changed. I learned that city strategy works better when selection criteria, data definitions, and review routines are designed together.

cards.title: Adapting a global member-reward idea to local markets
reach_out_when: You need to adapt a global loyalty idea to a market that behaves differently
You need a rough cost model before a finance model exists
cards.trigger: A member-reward idea designed globally needed checking for markets where members behave differently and the economics differ.
cards.problem: I couldn't just copy another market's settings. The design had to reward engagement, keep costs in check, and still work if the full product experience was delayed.
cards.method_and_execution: I built member groups, qualifying thresholds, and expected usage from local data, not borrowed assumptions. I costed optional and premium extras separately from the core reward. I wrote down every assumption that could be changed. I made a fallback using existing tools a deliberate choice, not an afterthought.
cards.artifacts: Decision frameworks, a cost simulator, validation checks, and an assumptions list.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that reusing an idea across markets means reusing the modelling approach, not the numbers. Premium extras should be costed and approved separately from the core design.

cards.title: Working out what member benefits really cost
reach_out_when: You need to turn scattered discount spend into a benefit members understand
A benefit risks concentrating spend on already-loyal users
cards.trigger: Proposed member benefits needed a clearer account of what they cost, what they replaced, and who would use them.
cards.problem: I had to explain how benefits would be paid for without claiming they cost nothing. I also had to stop costs growing automatically with the heaviest users.
cards.method_and_execution: I modelled moving existing spend as its own option, showing money freed up next to the total cost. For the heavy-user risk, I laid out product options: delaying eligibility, changing the value, capping use, or setting minimum order conditions. I compared these against how the heaviest users behave. When data sources disagreed, I showed the gap instead of forcing a single answer.
cards.artifacts: Cost controls built into decision models, cost sensitivity tables, and review checklists.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that claims about funding need the same care with sources and populations as customer numbers. Good benefits reward new behaviour rather than paying for what would happen anyway.

cards.title: Annual and midyear planning support
reach_out_when: You're preparing a planning cycle across several teams
You need to connect strategic themes to work people can deliver
cards.trigger: Each annual and midyear planning cycle, teams had to turn broad priorities into a clear set of discussions and inputs.
cards.problem: Plans came in at different levels of detail. Market context, team views, dependencies, and delivery questions needed to be considered together, not stitched together at the end.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped prepare for planning sessions and pulled inputs together into shared themes, keeping open questions visible. I used each cycle to check whether proposed work had a clear reason, known dependencies, and a practical path into day-to-day follow-up.
cards.artifacts: Planning deck, workshop agenda, roadmap, and decision memo.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that a good plan depends less on the amount of material and more on getting people aligned in the right order. Shared definitions, clear trade-offs, and reliable follow-up after workshops make a plan usable.

cards.title: Market entry strategy for battery-as-a-service
reach_out_when: You need to assess a battery-as-a-service market
You need to connect demand, unit economics, and launch choices
cards.trigger: I worked on whether battery-as-a-service (renting or subscribing to batteries instead of buying them) could make money in new markets.
cards.problem: The strategy had to tie together demand, customer needs, pricing, operations, and partner choices. A single adoption forecast was not enough.
cards.method_and_execution: I worked on market sizing, feasibility and profitability analysis, customer segments, and how to take the offer to market. I compared different business model assumptions and turned the research into choices about target customers, pricing, and rollout.
cards.artifacts: Market models, research decks, commercial scenarios, and strategy recommendations.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned to test business model assumptions against how things actually run. A promising technology needs a clear customer use and a believable path to making money repeatedly.

cards.title: Screening equity investments in beverages
reach_out_when: You need to screen investment targets in a consumer category
You need commercial due diligence to feed into valuation
cards.trigger: A Japanese beverage company was considering investing in India.
cards.problem: The decision depended on category demand, competition, how well each target fitted, and valuation assumptions.
cards.method_and_execution: I analysed the market and customers, shortlisted possible targets, supported early conversations and commercial due diligence, and built a valuation model.
cards.artifacts: A market screen, a target shortlist, due-diligence notes, and valuation scenarios.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned to spell out the investment case and valuation assumptions before narrowing down to one target.

cards.title: Integration planning after an FMCG acquisition
reach_out_when: You need an integration plan after an acquisition
You need process, organisation, and compliance work to line up
cards.trigger: After a cross-border acquisition, two businesses needed to combine their operations and teams.
cards.problem: The plan had to deal with overlapping processes, who would own what, milestones, and legal and tax requirements.
cards.method_and_execution: I worked with business leaders and specialist teams to simplify processes, design the new organisation, and plan the rollout.
cards.artifacts: An integration plan, milestones and success measures, and materials for the organisation workstream.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that integration needs named owners and a clear order of decisions, not just a savings target.

cards.title: Consumer satisfaction measurement program
reach_out_when: You want to set up regular satisfaction measurement
You need to turn survey feedback into questions for decision-makers
cards.trigger: Teams wanted a consistent way to see how consumer satisfaction was changing, and why.
cards.problem: A headline score on its own doesn't explain much. I needed to link it to the experiences behind it, without reading more into the survey than its design allowed.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped write survey questions, set up regular review meetings, and sort written and multiple-choice feedback into themes. I pushed for the same definitions and breakdowns over time. I pointed out what the data could and couldn't tell us, and presented findings as questions to dig into, not proof of cause.
cards.artifacts: Surveys, measurement workbooks, insight decks, research notes, and a regular review schedule.
cards.impact_or_learning: Teams got a shared, careful way to read consumer feedback and turn it into clear follow-up questions. I learned that satisfaction programs work best when they stay consistent over time but leave room to investigate.

cards.title: Grouping local areas for planning
reach_out_when: You need a practical way to group geographic areas
You need to translate location analysis into planning language
cards.trigger: Existing geographic boundaries didn't work well for consistent local planning and comparison.
cards.problem: We had detailed location data. The challenge was turning it into groups that made analytical sense and that planning teams could actually use. The method had to keep local context and still give a repeatable basis for comparison.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped build and document a clustering method and tested how different groupings behaved. I explained the logic to strategy colleagues in plain terms. I linked the technical ideas to practical questions about how teams define, compare, and discuss local areas.
cards.artifacts: Method document, analysis spreadsheet, data extract, and explainer deck.
cards.impact_or_learning: Later city discussions became easier to structure consistently. I learned that a location method is only useful when its assumptions are visible and its outputs map cleanly to real decisions.

cards.title: Targeting offers by customer history
reach_out_when: You need to replace one-size-fits-all offers with targeting by customer history
You need to check whether a model built elsewhere works in your market
cards.trigger: Offers were shown to broad audiences, with no account taken of past membership or how active people were.
cards.problem: With broad or suddenly changing audiences, it's hard to tell whether results came from demand, targeting, or how the campaign ran. Models built for other markets also needed checking before use here.
cards.method_and_execution: I turned analysis into targeting rules based on past membership, activity, and how likely people were to stay. I set out questions on refreshing audiences, exclusions, and clashing offers. For models built elsewhere, I wrote down their assumptions and noted which local conditions could make them fail.
cards.artifacts: Targeting frameworks, readiness checks, model-assumption reviews, and a market-fit table.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that personalisation only adds value when you can trace who got what and who was measured. Whether a model works in a new market depends on local economics as much as on accuracy.

cards.title: Designing reward challenges that can be measured
reach_out_when: You are designing goal-based rewards
Overlapping campaigns may spoil your control groups
A global programme needs decisions market by market
cards.trigger: Reward challenges (complete a goal, earn a reward) were used to build habits and encourage people to try other products.
cards.problem: Broad targeting risks paying for things people would do anyway. Audiences loading late made official start dates unreliable. Overlapping campaigns could spoil the comparison groups.
cards.method_and_execution: I measured readiness from the first time a customer actually saw the challenge. I required protection for both the test and comparison groups. I wrote down which campaign takes priority when they overlap. I argued for leaving out customers likely to act anyway, and kept engagement results separate from retention claims.
cards.artifacts: Campaign reviews, a checklist for who actually saw what, readiness checklists, and risk lists.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned to save a snapshot of each audience, record when people first see an offer, match rewards given against rewards used, and wait to scale until each group has a clean, complete result.

cards.title: Deciding which markets join global features
reach_out_when: A global feature needs different decisions for different markets
Features fit some markets in a region better than others
cards.trigger: Member features designed globally needed a clear decision about which markets in the region should take part.
cards.problem: Markets differ in demand, commercial setup, regulation, and ability to run tests that give clear answers. One decision for the whole region would have been wrong.
cards.method_and_execution: I coordinated a clear yes or no from each market, based on fit, what we'd learn, cost tolerance, and other changes happening at the same time. I challenged out-of-date status labels. I separated modelled estimates from real results, and required test plans and decision rules before scaling. For partner-funded offers, I turned manual campaign work into product and measurement requirements.
cards.artifacts: Decision briefs, market-fit tables, assessments of what each market can support, and readiness checks.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that a cheap test isn't automatically useful, and a local win doesn't prove something works across a whole market.

cards.title: Marketing strategy to attract Indian travellers to Japan
reach_out_when: You need to choose target audiences for destination marketing
You need to connect research with channel and content choices
cards.trigger: JNTO needed an approach built specifically for India to attract more travellers to Japan.
cards.problem: We had to work out which travellers were most promising, what appealed to them, and how they went from first hearing about Japan to planning a trip.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped build a picture of the market and travellers using consumer surveys, travel industry input, and expert interviews. The work linked traveller segments and their journeys to content themes, media channels, and a promotion plan.
cards.artifacts: A market study, traveller segment profiles, journey maps, content ideas, and a marketing plan.
cards.impact_or_learning: The key was linking evidence about the audience to a practical promotion plan, with local travel habits shaping the message and channel choices.

cards.title: Digitising freight management for a global manufacturer
reach_out_when: You need to scope a freight-management system
You need software selection to go hand in hand with process change
cards.trigger: A global manufacturer wanted its hubs to manage freight the same way.
cards.problem: Bidding, booking, tracking, choosing vendors, and getting people to use a new system were all linked. Treating them as separate technology tasks would not work.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped decide which system features mattered most, set up the vendor comparison, and worked out the process and change-management steps each team needed.
cards.artifacts: Requirements, vendor comparisons, an implementation plan, and performance measures.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that a new system only pays off when the way people work changes too. Picking the right product is not enough.

cards.title: Go-to-market strategy for a data-centre solution
reach_out_when: You need to position a new data-centre solution
You need to turn customer requirements into a sales approach
cards.trigger: A technology group explored offering an all-in-one data-centre solution in India.
cards.problem: Several product and service lines had to be packaged into one offer built around what customers needed.
cards.method_and_execution: I contributed to competitor, product, and customer research, and helped shape the offer, the target customers, and how to sell it.
cards.artifacts: Benchmarking, a customer-research plan, market positioning, and go-to-market materials.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that a service offer has to start from the customer's problem and how it will be delivered, not from bundling existing products.

cards.title: Monthly ANZ market-intelligence reports
reach_out_when: You want a regular market report with a clear structure
You need a report that's easier to keep running and hand over
cards.trigger: ANZ stakeholders wanted a regular picture of what was happening in the market, not scattered one-off updates.
cards.problem: Market news came from many places. The report had to give enough context to be useful, while staying short, comparable from month to month, and easy to keep running.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped gather inputs, group them into themes, check that claims were worded carefully, and tell a clear story about what changed and why it might matter. I also helped document the process so the report could continue when people moved on.
cards.artifacts: Monthly reports, presentation decks, trackers, briefing notes, and a handover guide.
cards.impact_or_learning: The report became a reusable tool that kept market context in front of planning discussions. I learned that regular reports help decisions when they answer the same key questions each time, rather than piling up updates.

cards.title: Case study of a competitor's market entry
reach_out_when: You need to turn a market event into a case study
You need lessons from a competitor's entry that apply elsewhere
cards.trigger: A competitor entered the market. It was a useful chance to study how positioning and market conditions interact.
cards.problem: The discussion needed to go beyond a timeline of events. The goal was to find lessons that could apply to other markets without overstating cause and effect.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped structure the case around context, visible moves, how others responded, and alternative explanations. I compared the phases of the entry and wrote down what was uncertain. I separated details specific to this market from broader questions we could reuse in future reviews.
cards.artifacts: Case-study deck, research notes, comparison tables, and a discussion guide.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that strong case studies keep the context rather than reducing events to a simple success or failure story. The work gave us a reusable way to study market entries and ask better questions before applying lessons elsewhere.

cards.title: Tracking the response to a competitor leaving the market
reach_out_when: A market event needs a structured response tracker
You need to turn a response into reusable lessons
cards.trigger: A competitor left the market. That raised fast-moving questions about how customers, merchants, and our operations would respond.
cards.problem: Teams needed one shared picture of what was changing, what each team was doing, and which observations were solid enough to act on later.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped set up a dated tracker that separated our actions from what we saw happening in the market. I kept assumptions written down as the situation changed. I helped pull together input from different teams. Afterwards, I looked back across the response to find patterns, gaps, and open questions.
cards.artifacts: Response trackers, summary decks, decision notes, and a look-back review.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that a response like this should keep both the timeline and the uncertainty. A disciplined tracker reduces conflicting stories during the event. A look-back review turns one-off coordination into lessons the team can reuse.

cards.title: Benchmarking against public company results
reach_out_when: You need a repeatable benchmark built from public sources
You need to separate real signals from differences in accounting
cards.trigger: Comparable businesses published regular results, which gave a useful but scattered view of how they were changing.
cards.problem: Different companies define their public numbers differently. I needed to compare them carefully without pretending unlike metrics were the same.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped set up regular reviews that checked source quality, definitions, and time periods, and kept facts separate from interpretation. I compared broad trends, wrote down caveats, and turned technical disclosures into short takeaways for internal discussion.
cards.artifacts: Benchmarking notes, comparison tables, and summaries for leadership.
cards.impact_or_learning: The team got a repeatable, careful way to discuss comparable businesses' public results. I learned that the most useful benchmark is often not a ranking, but a clear view of where comparisons hold and where they break down.

cards.title: Comparing competitor research across APAC markets
reach_out_when: You need to compare research resources across markets
You need an assessment that is honest about evidence quality
You need to turn scattered research into one regional view
cards.trigger: I wanted to understand how well competitor research could support consumer and membership decisions in each market across the region.
cards.problem: Markets had different research sources, definitions, update frequencies, and levels of quality. I needed a side-by-side view of what existed, how reliable it was, and what to improve. I also had to avoid treating missing information as proof that nothing existed.
cards.method_and_execution: I set up a common list of research types and put every market's inputs into the same format. I separated what was confirmed from what was only reported or still unclear. I grouped related items, noted how fresh and reliable each source was, and built a view of what to improve first. I kept local detail while making the comparison easy to scan.
cards.artifacts: A comparison table, a list of sources and their quality, a shared set of categories, and a priority list.
cards.impact_or_learning: Teams had a shared starting point for discussing research gaps and where to invest. I learned that a useful maturity view must show how good and how recent the evidence is, not just give a rating.

cards.title: Making member benefits easier to understand
reach_out_when: Members struggle to understand a benefit
You need a cost-neutral redesign with clear limits
cards.trigger: Some member value was real but hard for customers to notice or explain.
cards.problem: Complicated discounts can make value feel unclear. Simplifying a benefit, or using it to get people to try another product, has to keep costs in check. It also can't be presented as automatically giving more value.
cards.method_and_execution: I focused the redesign on whether customers understand the value and know where it came from, not just whether the numbers balance. I set limits on the total benefit budget. I asked product, finance, and legal colleagues to check feasibility, customer wording, and measurement before anything was agreed.
cards.artifacts: Customer-value write-ups, decision questions, and dependency lists.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that cost-neutral on paper doesn't mean ready to launch. How the benefit is delivered, whether customers understand it, the wording, who gets it, and how it's measured all need checking separately.

cards.title: Measuring consumer affordability
reach_out_when: You need to talk about affordability without relying on one metric
You need a method for comparing what customers pay
cards.trigger: Teams needed a clearer way to talk about what customers actually pay across different kinds of orders.
cards.problem: Affordability isn't one displayed price. What customers experience depends on what they order, fees, promotions, and what they compare against, and all of these change.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped design a measurement approach with explicit definitions that broke the price experience into its parts. I tested whether comparisons still made sense over time and in different situations. I also explained the model in plain language so people could question the assumptions instead of treating the index as a black box.
cards.artifacts: Measurement models, research notes, method explainers, and review summaries.
cards.impact_or_learning: The team got a reusable way to discuss consumer value carefully, without reducing it to an unsupported headline. I learned that affordability measures are more useful when their assumptions are visible and they can answer several different questions.

cards.title: Analysing the response to a competitor promotion
reach_out_when: A competitor promotion needs a measured response
You need to monitor customer groups before deciding to act
cards.trigger: A major competitor ran a big promotion. Leaders wanted to know how exposed our customers were and how strongly we should respond.
cards.problem: I needed to tell real competitive pressure apart from normal ups and downs, and show which customer groups and parts of the experience needed a closer look.
cards.method_and_execution: I analysed customer behaviour and grouped customers by how exposed they were. I helped lay out response options with clear trade-offs. I also helped set up monitoring that separated routine watching from the signs that would justify stronger action, and kept open risks in front of leadership.
cards.artifacts: Analysis readouts, customer groupings, a scenario model, a monitoring plan, and a leadership deck.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that a credible response does not have to be immediate or broad. Evidence by customer group, clear trigger points, and honest caveats made it easier to watch the situation and discuss a proportionate response.

cards.title: Fuel costs and consumer behaviour
reach_out_when: You need to turn an outside trend into clear questions about consumers
You want a careful, method-first view of a market change
cards.trigger: Fuel prices were changing, and people asked how consumers might change their behaviour across rides and delivery.
cards.problem: It was tempting to assume that because two things happened at the same time, one caused the other. I needed to turn the news into careful questions instead.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped review the fuel price trend and listed the ways consumers might plausibly respond. I separated what we could see right away from what would need deeper checking. I treated other explanations as part of the analysis and kept the questions broad enough to test against our own data later.
cards.artifacts: A research note and a tracker for the fuel price signal.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that big economic trends are good prompts but weak conclusions on their own. It helps to spell out how the trend would change behaviour, list other explanations, and decide what evidence would change your mind.

cards.title: Buy now, pay later in food delivery
reach_out_when: You're assessing a payment offer next to your core business
You need a short research brief before deeper analysis
cards.trigger: I contributed to looking at how deferred-payment options (buy now, pay later) might fit into the food-delivery customer experience.
cards.problem: I wanted to separate a broad payments trend from the questions that matter for on-demand delivery: whether customers would care, how it would fit operationally, and what it might cost the experience.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped break the topic into testable questions, reviewed available material, and summarised what we found in a short strategic note. I didn't treat take-up elsewhere as proof it would work here, and kept the unknowns visible so later work could focus on the biggest gaps.
cards.artifacts: A research note and a working model.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that assessing a new adjacent area is most useful when it spells out what would need to be true, rather than rushing to a recommendation. That makes it easier to move from an interesting trend to proper product or market investigation.

cards.title: Brand-level checks within categories
reach_out_when: You need brand-level analysis without exposing partner details
You need a consistent way to compare accounts
cards.trigger: Category averages were hiding real differences in how individual brands showed up on the platform.
cards.problem: I needed a more detailed view without turning it into a league table, or implying that every difference had the same cause.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped set up checks using the same measures and time periods for every brand, with clear caveats. I reviewed patterns across brands and linked them to the wider category. I listed follow-up questions for colleagues with local knowledge to dig into.
cards.artifacts: Analysis workbooks, brand briefs, comparison views, and discussion notes.
cards.impact_or_learning: The team got a practical way to spot where deeper investigation might help, without sharing sensitive partner detail or unsupported performance claims. I learned that brand-level analysis is most credible with a consistent structure that still leaves room for different local situations.

cards.title: ANZ membership coverage analysis
reach_out_when: You need to compare member and non-member experiences
You need a coverage analysis that doesn't rely on detailed numbers
You need to explain a membership opportunity without exposing restricted metrics
cards.trigger: I wanted to understand where membership was strong across the ANZ consumer experience, and where we still had gaps in our picture.
cards.problem: I needed a consistent way to compare members and non-members without boiling it down to one number. I also had to separate overall coverage from differences caused by location, restaurant choice, or consumer behaviour.
cards.method_and_execution: I built a structured comparison of members and non-members, checked how the picture changed across markets and situations, and turned the findings into questions for decision-makers. I focused on where teams should look next, and kept sensitive performance detail out of wide circulation.
cards.artifacts: An analysis pack, a diagnostic framework, and a decision brief.
cards.impact_or_learning: Membership coverage became a clearer input to strategy instead of a one-off report. I learned to treat availability, relevance, and engagement as separate problems rather than lumping them together.

cards.title: Setting up tests for recurring member benefits
reach_out_when: You need to test a simple recurring member benefit cleanly
Several benefit ideas risk being tested as one bundle
cards.trigger: Several possible member benefits were being explored at the same time.
cards.problem: Different ideas risked being mixed up with each other. An attractive but unfinished idea also risked holding up the main roadmap.
cards.method_and_execution: I made clear what each benefit was and wasn't testing. I helped set up separate and combined test groups, and pushed for clean control groups when related tests weren't ready. I treated early rollouts as a check that things worked, not as proof of customer impact.
cards.artifacts: Decision briefs, test comparisons, readiness checks, and a measurement plan.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that even simple customer benefits need careful sign-up, scope, and evidence rules. Keeping related ideas separate lets the main roadmap move on its own.

cards.title: How to make money from a connected-car service
reach_out_when: You need to turn a connected-product idea into a business model
You need to test usage and revenue assumptions together
cards.trigger: I worked on how a connected-car service could keep delivering value to customers and support a workable business model.
cards.problem: The offer had to connect how often people would use it, how the service was designed, and the financial assumptions. A list of features would not guarantee people kept using it.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped outline possible customer offers, ways to keep users engaged, and ways to charge for the service. I then tested what each option meant through financial forecasts and scenario discussions.
cards.artifacts: Business model options, engagement ideas, financial forecasts, and strategy decks.
cards.impact_or_learning: The work confirmed that revenue follows repeated customer value. Usage assumptions and revenue forecasts have to be looked at together.

cards.title: Software concept for large-scale energy storage
reach_out_when: You need to define a digital product around a complex energy workflow
You need to turn market and user research into software requirements
cards.trigger: I worked on the idea for software to help run large battery storage sites for power grids, getting the most out of the storage and managing revenue.
cards.problem: Before deciding what the software should do, the team needed to connect business goals, day-to-day workflows, what competitors offered, and what users needed.
cards.method_and_execution: I worked on comparing the market and existing software, interviewing stakeholders, mapping processes, and ranking the features that mattered most. The work helped set the direction for development and the questions to answer before choosing a vendor or building.
cards.artifacts: Competitor comparisons, process maps, feature lists, concept decks, and development planning material.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that a good product idea starts with the decisions and workflows it supports. Feature lists mean more when the business process and assumptions behind them are clear.

cards.title: Screening renewable-energy investment opportunities
reach_out_when: You need to compare renewable-energy investment markets
You need to go from a market overview to a shortlist of companies to approach
cards.trigger: An energy investor wanted to find promising renewable-energy opportunities in India and other Asian markets.
cards.problem: An attractive market was not enough. Policy, economics, possible partners, and strategic fit all mattered.
cards.method_and_execution: I researched market conditions and technology options, helped screen and shortlist companies, and supported early conversations to test fit.
cards.artifacts: Market screens, target lists, research reports, and discussion materials.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned to use a broad market scan to decide what to investigate next, not as the final investment decision.

cards.title: Business plan for a two-wheeler finance arm
reach_out_when: You need to assess an in-house finance arm for a vehicle maker
You need finance products that fit customer and dealer needs
cards.trigger: A two-wheeler manufacturer looked at whether its own finance business could help customers buy and improve results.
cards.problem: The idea needed a viable customer group, loan terms, a partner structure, and the ability to run it.
cards.method_and_execution: I contributed to the feasibility study, customer and competitor analysis, questions about the product and how it would run, and a phased business plan.
cards.artifacts: Feasibility reports, customer research, business-model options, and implementation plans.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that a finance business has to balance customer value, risk, dealer operations, and the ability to collect repayments.

cards.title: Cost-reduction programme for an automotive business
reach_out_when: You need to find cost savings across an automotive value chain
You need to turn a benchmark into an action plan
cards.trigger: An automotive business wanted to find lasting cost savings.
cards.problem: A believable programme needed comparisons across functions and a focus on initiatives that could actually be delivered.
cards.method_and_execution: I benchmarked costs along the automotive value chain, found where performance lagged, and helped plan a multi-part cost-reduction programme.
cards.artifacts: A benchmark, a map of savings opportunities, and a cost-reduction roadmap.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that a benchmark becomes useful when each opportunity has an owner, a timeline, and a clear view of practical limits.

cards.title: Vehicle demand forecasting and supply-chain planning
reach_out_when: You need a more detailed vehicle-demand forecast
You need forecasting that feeds directly into inventory decisions
cards.trigger: An automotive manufacturer needed a better basis for planning supply and inventory.
cards.problem: Demand varied by region and product features, so one broad forecast could not guide day-to-day decisions.
cards.method_and_execution: I combined bottom-up and top-down forecasts broken down by region and product, and set up a process of regular improvement for supply and inventory planning.
cards.artifacts: A forecast model, regional and product breakdowns, inventory recommendations, and a regular review schedule.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned to make forecast assumptions visible and tie each model update to the decision it should improve.

cards.title: Research on electric vehicle policy and industry in India
reach_out_when: You need to understand how policy shapes an emerging mobility market
You need to connect regulatory research with business choices
cards.trigger: I worked on policy and industry questions about electric mobility in India.
cards.problem: Investment and rollout choices depended on a changing mix of regulation, infrastructure, industry incentives, and the interests of different groups.
cards.method_and_execution: I worked on reviewing regulations, mapping the market and key players, and summarising how policy changes might affect business options. Where implementation or timing was uncertain, I helped present findings as scenarios and questions for decision-makers.
cards.artifacts: Policy notes, market studies, stakeholder maps, and presentations.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that policy research is more valuable when it explains which practical choices it changes and is open about uncertainty in how policies will be carried out.

cards.title: Strategy for a blockchain-based mobility platform
reach_out_when: You need to test whether blockchain fits a real mobility problem
You need to compare platform and product business models
cards.trigger: A mobility platform idea needed a way for different operators to share data and handle transactions with each other.
cards.problem: The strategy had to show where the technology actually solved a business problem, which partners were needed, and how it could grow.
cards.method_and_execution: I looked at the regulatory and technology questions, mapped possible partners, and compared platform and product options alongside the market and business model.
cards.artifacts: A feasibility assessment, a partner map, business-model options, and a strategy deck.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned to judge a new technology by the coordination problem it solves and whether partners actually want to take part.

cards.title: India–Japan trade and industry competitiveness analysis
reach_out_when: You need to turn trade data into negotiation questions
You need a structured view of sector competitiveness
cards.trigger: A project for the Japanese government needed evidence on India's trade position and how competitive its industries were.
cards.problem: The analysis had to connect big-picture trade patterns with barriers in specific sectors and possible policy responses.
cards.method_and_execution: I worked on research and coordination covering trade data, industry structure, policy comparisons, and stakeholder input. The outputs set out discussion points and recommendations for policy talks between India and Japan.
cards.artifacts: Trade and sector analysis, meeting decks, policy notes, and symposium material.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned to separate what the data showed from what policy negotiations could realistically achieve. Work across governments also depends on careful coordination and giving proper credit.

cards.title: Launch checks for membership platform and web page changes
reach_out_when: A platform change needs proof it works before launch
A public page must match a product change accurately
cards.trigger: Changes to our membership offers system and public product pages had to match what customers would actually see.
cards.problem: Setting up an offer in the system did not prove it would show correctly to customers. A correct draft web page was not enough either, because different customer groups switched over at different times.
cards.method_and_execution: I split "it is set up" from "we have seen it work". I held launches until each test had a named owner, live evidence, and someone accountable for fixing faults. For public pages, I mapped who needed to review them, kept unconfirmed content from being published by mistake, and asked for previews in each local language before anything was scheduled.
cards.artifacts: Test evidence requirements, go/no-go checklists, reviewer maps, and pre-publishing checklists.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that a change is only done when you can see it working for customers. Public page updates should be run like small launches, each with a clear owner.

cards.title: Regular market-intelligence review meetings
reach_out_when: You want a light, regular routine for reviewing market news
You need to separate important developments from background noise
cards.trigger: The market was moving fast, and the strategy team needed a dependable routine for reviewing what was happening.
cards.problem: There was a constant stream of outside news. The meetings had to be timely without treating every change as strategically important.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped review new developments, group related ones, pick questions worth deeper analysis, and bring short context into regular discussions. I helped set up a way of working that kept what we observed separate from what we thought it meant, and was clear about uncertainty.
cards.artifacts: Review notes, intelligence summaries, trackers, and discussion briefs.
cards.impact_or_learning: The team got better at noticing changes early and sending the most useful questions on to deeper strategy work. I learned that good market intelligence is less about collecting everything and more about consistent judgement on what matters and how confident we are.

cards.title: Working with a remote analytics team
reach_out_when: You need a working routine with a remote analytics team
Analytics requests need clearer priorities and feedback
cards.trigger: I worked with an analytics team based elsewhere. We needed a regular way to agree priorities, clarify requests, and review their work.
cards.problem: Business questions often got lost on the way to becoming analysis. Context, priorities, and feedback had to cross team boundaries.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped run frequent check-ins where everyone could see the request queue. For each request, we agreed what decision the analysis would support. I helped separate urgent questions from longer-term foundational work. We used feedback to write better requests over time.
cards.artifacts: Priority tracker, request brief template, meeting format, and handover notes.
cards.impact_or_learning: Requests became clearer and easier to deliver. I learned that remote teams work best when both sides agree what a good request and a good review look like. Clear context, tight scope, and quick feedback cut rework more than extra process does.

cards.title: Aligning market priorities for membership
reach_out_when: You need to reconcile regional and market priorities
You need a clear pre-read for a planning discussion
You need to bring hidden assumptions into the open before escalating
cards.trigger: Market teams' membership priorities needed to be lined up before they went into regional planning and product discussions.
cards.problem: Markets described their needs in different levels of detail and with different assumptions about timing, ownership, and evidence. I needed to keep local context while making the requests easy to compare.
cards.method_and_execution: I put every market request into the same format: the customer problem, the decision needed, dependencies, how developed the idea was, and the owner. I separated confirmed needs from guesses and pointed out conflicts and missing evidence. I ran working sessions to refine them. Where teams could not agree, I recorded the open decision instead of forcing agreement.
cards.artifacts: An alignment brief, a prioritisation template, a decision log, and a workshop pre-read.
cards.impact_or_learning: Regional and market teams could discuss priorities from the same starting point. I learned that alignment does not mean agreeing on everything. It means being clear on what is known, what is disputed, and who decides next.

cards.title: Business-review reporting process
reach_out_when: A regular review pack takes too much effort to maintain
You need to make reporting easier to hand over
cards.trigger: Regular business reviews needed a more repeatable path from raw updates to a clear story for leadership.
cards.problem: Putting the pack together was manual and repetitive, inputs were inconsistent, and the know-how sat with only a few people.
cards.method_and_execution: I supported producing the reviews, wrote down the recurring steps, and looked for places where standard templates or automation could save effort. I also put together handover material so someone else could follow the steps, checks, and story structure without needing it explained in person.
cards.artifacts: Business-review deck, reporting template, process documentation, and handover guide.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that automating reporting works best once the process is written down clearly. A repeatable template, clear check points, and notes on judgement calls matter as much as automating the mechanical steps.

cards.title: Regular restaurants and retail strategy meeting
reach_out_when: You need to set up a regular review for a business area
You want recurring discussions to lead to clear follow-ups
cards.trigger: Restaurants and retail work needed a regular meeting that linked weekly priorities to the wider business reviews.
cards.problem: Without it, these topics were discussed in separate meetings, with no consistent link between immediate delivery questions and longer-term planning.
cards.method_and_execution: I supported a regular meeting that grouped updates, highlighted dependencies, and made room to revisit priorities over different time horizons. I focused on making the discussion easy to follow and carrying open questions forward, adjusting the level of detail to the audience.
cards.artifacts: A meeting schedule and format, business-review deck, and action tracker.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that a useful regular meeting isn't just a series of get-togethers. It needs a consistent storyline, clear follow-up, and a clear split between sharing information, solving problems, and making decisions.

cards.title: Running a regular product and operations meeting for membership
reach_out_when: You need a useful regular meeting between product and operations
Dependencies are getting lost between teams
A recurring meeting needs clearer decisions and follow-through
cards.trigger: Regional operations and product teams needed a reliable place to review membership dependencies and make decisions together.
cards.problem: Updates were scattered across separate workstreams. Regular meetings could easily turn into status updates with no decisions. I needed a format that made owners, escalations, and follow-ups clear, while respecting what each team was responsible for.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped set a recurring agenda built around decisions, dependencies, launches, and open questions. I brought short pre-reads, made clear what outcome each topic needed, and recorded owners and next steps. I also brought market context into the meeting and took product guidance back to the market teams.
cards.artifacts: A meeting format, an agenda template, a decision log, and an action tracker.
cards.impact_or_learning: The meeting became more about decisions than status updates. I learned these meetings work best when every agenda item names the decision or dependency it is meant to resolve.

cards.title: Regular updates for APAC Central Operations
reach_out_when: You need a repeatable format for regional updates
Important context is scattered across workstreams
You want leadership updates to be short and actionable
cards.trigger: Regional operations stakeholders needed to keep track of changing priorities and dependencies across many workstreams.
cards.problem: Updates came through different meetings at different levels of detail. Readers struggled to see what had changed, what needed attention, and where a decision was waiting. I needed a short, regular update that added to meetings rather than repeating them.
cards.method_and_execution: I organised updates around decisions, progress, risks, and upcoming requests. I wrote them in plain language, kept information separate from actions, and used the same structure each time so people could skim. I checked uncertain items with the people who owned them before sending anything widely.
cards.artifacts: A newsletter, short pulse updates, briefing notes, and a communications calendar.
cards.impact_or_learning: Regional context became easier to take in and act on. I learned that a good internal update saves the reader interpretation work, while staying clear about what's uncertain and who owns what.

cards.title: Handing over my ANZ strategy and planning role
reach_out_when: You are planning a role transition
You need to turn a broad role into a clear handover
You need recurring strategy work to continue smoothly
cards.trigger: I was moving from an ANZ strategy and planning role into a regional consumer role. I wanted to leave the work in good shape for the next person.
cards.problem: A list of open tasks was not enough. The new owner needed to know which decisions came up regularly, what stakeholders expected, which reports and analyses existed, and which questions still needed judgement.
cards.method_and_execution: I organised the role by workstream and wrote down the purpose and timing of each. I separated finished work from open decisions and listed every report and dashboard the team used. I also flagged dependencies, access the new owner would need, and assumptions they should re-check rather than take on trust.
cards.artifacts: A handover document, a workstream list, a dashboard list, and a transition checklist.
cards.impact_or_learning: The new owner could get up to speed without relying on hallway knowledge. The lesson: a good handover explains how decisions get made, not just where the files are.

cards.title: Choosing which Southeast Asian markets to enter for cosmetics
reach_out_when: You need to choose among Southeast Asian markets to enter
You need to adapt a beauty offer to different countries
cards.trigger: A diversified Japanese beauty group explored expanding in Southeast Asia.
cards.problem: Country choices had to reflect market growth, category trends, what consumers wanted, and whether one regional approach could work.
cards.method_and_execution: I researched economic and cosmetics trends, compared priority countries, and helped shape a regional go-to-market plan.
cards.artifacts: Country screens, a market model, consumer insights, and go-to-market recommendations.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that a regional strategy needs shared criteria while still respecting differences between countries.

cards.title: Reusing and recycling EV batteries
reach_out_when: You need to assess second-life uses for batteries
You need to compare reuse and recycling partners
cards.trigger: An automotive client wanted to know how batteries could keep creating value after their life in a vehicle.
cards.problem: Possible reuses, technical requirements, policy, and recycling options all had to be assessed together.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped screen possible second-life uses, reviewed customer and policy requirements, and assessed potential recycling partners.
cards.artifacts: A map of reuse opportunities, policy analysis, a partner shortlist, and research materials.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned to separate how valuable a reuse idea is from what it takes to deploy it safely and handle batteries at end of life.

cards.title: Screening next-generation battery technologies
reach_out_when: You need to compare emerging battery technologies
You need a structured way to choose R&D investments
cards.trigger: A trading company's R&D team wanted to find battery technologies that could become commercially useful.
cards.problem: The technologies differed in maturity, cost, use, demand, and competition, so no single performance measure could rank them fairly.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped assess each option against practical and commercial criteria and built a ranking of which ones to investigate further.
cards.artifacts: A technology landscape, evaluation criteria, a prioritisation matrix, and a research deck.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned to spell out assumptions about maturity and commercial readiness when comparing technologies at different stages.

cards.title: Reorganising teams to deliver a data-centre offer
reach_out_when: You need several business units to deliver one service
You need a phased plan for organisational change
cards.trigger: The new data-centre offer needed business units that had always sold separate products to work together.
cards.problem: One joined-up service needed clear responsibilities, incentives, sales processes, and a step-by-step transition.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped design how the future organisation would work, compared competitors, and planned how to bring stakeholders along and manage the change.
cards.artifacts: An organisation blueprint, a transformation roadmap, a stakeholder plan, and an operating-model deck.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that a joined-up offer to customers depends on internal ownership and incentives that support it.

cards.title: Car buyer segments and pricing research
reach_out_when: You need to understand car buyer segments
You need to connect pricing evidence with product and marketing decisions
cards.trigger: I worked on consumer studies to support decisions on car models, pricing, and marketing.
cards.problem: Teams needed to understand how customers differed in needs, buying journeys, and willingness to pay, rather than relying on an "average" customer.
cards.method_and_execution: I worked on both qualitative and quantitative research, including interviews, surveys, in-home observation, and pricing exercises. I helped turn the findings into customer segment profiles, journey maps, and what they meant for decisions, while being clear about the limits of the samples and methods.
cards.artifacts: Surveys and interview guides, segment profiles, customer journeys, pricing analyses, and client decks.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned to use segmentation as a tool for making choices. The useful output is a clear picture of how different customers behave and what that means for the product, message, or sales channel.

cards.title: Choosing sales channels for a sunscreen launch
reach_out_when: You need to choose channels for a consumer-product launch
You need to match customer groups with distribution partners
cards.trigger: A Japanese personal-care company explored launching sunscreen in India.
cards.problem: The way to reach customers had to suit different customer groups, how they shop, and the economics of each channel.
cards.method_and_execution: I researched consumers, compared competitors, assessed distribution options, and developed a channel strategy with potential partners.
cards.artifacts: Consumer segments, a channel map, competitor analysis, and market-entry recommendations.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned to design channels around how customers actually buy, rather than assuming one route works nationwide.

cards.title: Repositioning a skincare brand in the US
reach_out_when: You need to reposition a skincare brand
You need to turn category research into a distinct offer
cards.trigger: A Japanese skincare group reviewed how its brand was positioned in the United States.
cards.problem: The work had to cover category trends, channels, competitors, and why customers chose or rejected the brand.
cards.method_and_execution: I contributed to market and competitor research and helped turn what we learned about the category and customers into positioning and product questions.
cards.artifacts: A category overview, competitor maps, a SWOT, product benchmarking, and recommendations.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned to test what makes a brand different against how customers talk and how competitors are sold.

cards.title: Supporting an electric three-wheeler battery-swap pilot
reach_out_when: You need to move a mobility idea into a real-world pilot
You need practical pilot management across several partners
cards.trigger: I supported a pilot where electric three-wheelers swapped batteries at stations. It needed the vehicle, charging, station, and operations teams to work together.
cards.problem: The pilot would only teach us something useful if readiness, daily operations, problems, and partner responsibilities were all tracked in one place.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped run the project management: timelines, partner coordination, resource planning, reporting, and reviews of operating issues. I helped organise the evidence into a clear view of what the pilot tested and what was still unresolved.
cards.artifacts: Pilot plans, operations trackers, partner updates, and a final report.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that pilots are as much about careful observation and fixing problems as about how the technology performs. Clear owners and a shared record of what happened make later decisions about scaling more credible.

cards.title: Pilot to improve customer experience at car dealerships
reach_out_when: You need to test a change to the dealership experience
You need to connect process, people, and tools in a frontline pilot
cards.trigger: I supported an effort to improve how an automotive dealership network engaged with customers.
cards.problem: Advice on better customer experience had to turn into what frontline staff actually did, how managers ran things, and tools that worked.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped design and run a pilot using a plan-do-check-act approach: try a change, check the results, adjust. The work covered roles, training, recognition, and changes to processes and tools. We recorded what we learned to guide later decisions.
cards.artifacts: Pilot plans, process maps, training material, review decks, and action trackers.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that frontline change needs clear owners and regular feedback. A strategy only becomes testable when it turns into daily actions reviewed with the people doing the work.

cards.title: Co-branding strategy to reach millennials for a legacy car brand
reach_out_when: You need to choose a co-branding partner
You need to turn a partnership idea into a campaign plan
cards.trigger: A legacy automotive brand wanted to appeal to younger customers.
cards.problem: The right partner needed an overlapping audience and a good brand fit, followed by a practical plan for campaigns and measuring results.
cards.method_and_execution: I assessed potential partner brands, helped set the criteria for a good fit, and developed a roadmap for joint commercial and marketing work.
cards.artifacts: A partner shortlist, brand-fit analysis, a campaign roadmap, and a way to evaluate results.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that co-branding needs a believable link between the two audiences and a clear plan for what happens after the announcement.

cards.title: Reviewing the scope of my strategy role
reach_out_when: You're taking stock of a broad strategy role
You need to explain how different pieces of work fit together
cards.trigger: My strategy and planning work had grown broad, and I needed a clear picture of what I was responsible for.
cards.problem: I wanted to explain a varied set of work without reducing it to a task list, and without relying on restricted goals or performance numbers.
cards.method_and_execution: I grouped my work into long-running themes and mapped the regular meetings and deliverables involved. I looked at how short-term requests related to ongoing responsibilities. This helped me spot overlaps, make unspoken expectations easier to discuss, and show where my time was going.
cards.artifacts: A scope deck and a tracker of my work.
cards.impact_or_learning: I learned that reviewing your scope from time to time is a practical tool, not just a look back. It shows where work is scattered, separates reactive from strategic work, and makes it easier to prioritise and hand over later.

cards.title: Weekly tracking of market promotions
reach_out_when: You need a repeatable way to track promotions
You want to turn noisy market observations into useful themes
cards.trigger: Promotions in the market were changing often, and the team needed to track them properly rather than rely on one-off observations.
cards.problem: Tracking changing activity consistently week to week is hard. The work needed to keep useful context without jumping to conclusions from single examples.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped run a weekly process to collect and review promotions, and grouped what we saw into comparable themes. I flagged where an apparent pattern needed more evidence. I kept the tracker focused on what mattered strategically, not on every detail.
cards.artifacts: A weekly tracker, summary brief, review deck, and collection template.
cards.impact_or_learning: The team could discuss patterns over time and pick out questions worth deeper work. I learned that frequent tracking is most useful as a reliable memory of the market, not a trigger to react to every change.

cards.title: Data foundations for market intelligence
reach_out_when: Your market data needs clear definitions and checks
You want to turn regular data pulls into files that are easy to maintain
cards.trigger: Our regular market-intelligence work needed more consistent data and tracking files.
cards.problem: There was a gap between receiving new information and keeping a reliable history of it. We needed clear definitions, notes on where data came from, and checks so repeat analysis didn't depend on someone's memory.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped organise datasets and extracts, write down how each input should be read, and review tracking outputs. I set up files so analysts could tell raw sources, processed data, and presentation apart, without claiming more certainty than the evidence allowed.
cards.artifacts: Datasets, trackers, data dictionaries, dashboard specifications, and review notes.
cards.impact_or_learning: Tracking became easier to maintain, and refreshing regular analyses caused less confusion. I learned that good intelligence depends on quiet groundwork: stable definitions, knowing where data came from, and repeatable checks.

cards.title: Comparing menu and in-store prices
reach_out_when: You need a defensible way to compare prices
You need to document the limits of a market measurement
cards.trigger: Strategy teams needed a consistent way to compare prices on menus with prices in store.
cards.problem: Prices were collected through different channels, in different formats, at different times. The hard part was comparing them consistently, not any single price.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped design the measurement approach, define which observations could be compared, write down exclusions and caveats, and organise repeated data collection. I helped keep observed differences separate from interpretation, so people understood what the method could and couldn't show.
cards.artifacts: A measurement framework, collection template, tracker, and research note.
cards.impact_or_learning: The team could discuss relative pricing without false precision, and with the limitations in plain view. I learned that price comparisons are most credible when the matching rules, timing, and handling of missing data are spelled out.

cards.title: Tracking restaurant selection and coverage
reach_out_when: You need a repeatable view of restaurant selection and coverage
You need to agree on metric definitions before reviewing gaps
cards.trigger: Teams needed a consistent view of which restaurants were on the platform and where the gaps were, across markets.
cards.problem: Teams used different definitions, data sources, and reporting expectations. I had to line these up so gaps could be compared fairly.
cards.method_and_execution: I helped build regular files with clear metric definitions, routine quality checks, and transparent handling of exceptions. I helped with comparison reviews, wrote down the reporting logic, and organised outputs so market teams could tell data problems apart from real selection gaps.
cards.artifacts: Workbooks, dashboard views, metric definitions, comparison checks, and notes on how definitions are managed.
cards.impact_or_learning: Coverage reviews became repeatable, with less confusion from inconsistent breakdowns or changing data. I learned that selection reporting is more actionable when keeping definitions consistent is treated as part of the job.

cards.title: Planning updates to public product pages
reach_out_when: You need to plan a public product-page update
A page change depends on several reviewers
You need to separate content approval from being ready to build
cards.trigger: Public product pages needed updating alongside wider product and customer-communication changes.
cards.problem: A page update involved more than writing text. Product facts, translation, legal review, who builds it, and launch timing all had to line up. Pages for new customers also had to stay separate from what signed-in customers see.
cards.method_and_execution: I mapped who approves and who builds, and which sections needed specialist help. I put review, preview, and go-live checks in order. I wrote down open product and timing questions instead of filling gaps with guesses. I made it clear what 'ready to plan' meant versus 'ready to publish'.
cards.artifacts: Update plan, review checklist, go-live plan, and owner map.
cards.impact_or_learning: There was a clearer path from a product decision to a checked page change, without claiming anything was delivered before it was confirmed. I learned to treat web updates as small launches, with clear owners for facts, wording, build, and timing.

cards.title: Self-service campaign tracking and spend estimation
reach_out_when: Local teams can't see how campaigns are going
Reward spend is hard to estimate
cards.trigger: Local teams relied on central staff to find out who saw a campaign, how it was going, and what it would likely cost.
cards.problem: A self-service tool needed to make this visible without giving false precision, especially when late data and overlapping campaigns made the raw numbers unreliable.
